Code: Caregiver memory is part of the regimen
Definition: Caregivers themselves often track schedules through habit and memory, so family support is not an error-free external safety layer.
Subtheme: Care work and reminders circulate through relationships and presence
Theme: Medication work is relationally distributed, while agency and authority remain differentiated
Example_quote: "I just remember on my own!... it’s just become a habit from taking them and giving them every single day." (C05, Phase 1, L27)
Reflexivity_note: This counters an implicit assumption that shifting responsibility to a caregiver necessarily removes memory-related vulnerability.
Interview_gap: C05 was not probed on handover, checking, or role origin, so this code concerns her own memory practice only.

Definition: One caregiver described responsibility becoming routine without a formal household decision.
Subtheme: Care work and reminders circulate through relationships and presence
Theme: Medication work is relationally distributed, while agency and authority remain differentiated
Example_quote: "It mostly just happened. I started helping because they needed it, and then it became my routine." (C01, Phase 1, L357)
Reflexivity_note: I demoted the former general theme because only C01 directly supports it.
Interview_gap: Directly supported by C01 only; the protocol's role-origin question was not consistently asked, so do not generalize how caregiver roles originate.

Definition: Whoever is nearby may remind, so responsibility moves with household presence.
Subtheme: Care work and reminders circulate through relationships and presence
Theme: Medication work is relationally distributed, while agency and authority remain differentiated
Example_quote: "Somebody sees. Somebody reminds. Somebody checks. It is like that."
Reflexivity_note: This is circulation, not evidence that nobody carries primary responsibility.

Definition: Families discuss options, but participants reserve medication changes for clinicians.
Subtheme: Knowledge, interpretation, supply, and clinical authority sit with different people
Theme: Medication work is relationally distributed, while agency and authority remain differentiated
Example_quote: "It should help us remember and understand. Doctor is still doctor."
Reflexivity_note: Peer influence does not erase the consistently stated clinical boundary.

Definition: Pharmacists translate difficult prescriptions and identify medicines without taking prescribing authority.
Subtheme: Knowledge, interpretation, supply, and clinical authority sit with different people
Theme: Medication work is relationally distributed, while agency and authority remain differentiated
Example_quote: "The pharmacist usually understands it." (C02, Phase 1, L157)
Reflexivity_note: I retained pharmacists because the care network extends beyond co residents.

Definition: Repeated positive accounts from family, friends, or peers can increase confidence in a medicine while participants still distinguish that influence from clinical authorization.
Subtheme: Knowledge, interpretation, supply, and clinical authority sit with different people
Theme: Medication work is relationally distributed, while agency and authority remain differentiated
Example_quote: "If I am with a group and everyone says they take some medicine... I may feel that medicine is more trustworthy."
Reflexivity_note: The interviews repeatedly prompted group-opinion hypotheticals; retain as contextual evidence but do not make it a headline finding.
Interview_gap: Some group-influence questions were leading and repeated; use only to bound trust/authority claims.

Definition: Older adults may retain dosing while kin handle identification, supply, or interpretation.
Subtheme: Older adults preserve practical agency through routine, recognition, and selective independence
Theme: Medication work is relationally distributed, while agency and authority remain differentiated
Example_quote: "They are not completely dependent on me. They can take the medicine."
Reflexivity_note: I separated taking from knowing to avoid treating distributed work as dependence.

Definition: Caregivers worry when they cannot check while managing other work.
Subtheme: Checking carries care, worry, and relational pressure at the same time
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "If nobody checks then I worry. So it is pressure." (C03, Phase 1, L49)
Reflexivity_note: Caregiver accounts may justify oversight, so the older adult boundary remains necessary.
Interview_gap: Caregiver worry was not directly probed in most transcripts; avoid frequency claims.

Definition: A concerning missed-dose episode can change a household from assuming self-management to more active reminders and checking.
Subtheme: Checking carries care, worry, and relational pressure at the same time
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "Before that we just assumed he will remember... Now I feel maybe we should not depend only on memory." (C03, Phase 1, L41)
Reflexivity_note: The reported health episode is temporal context, not proof that the missed dose caused the later symptoms.
Interview_gap: Directly supported in C03; do not generalize a universal escalation trajectory from one household.

Definition: Caregivers away from home cannot observe whether a dose occurred.
Subtheme: Handoffs and distance create uncertainty about what actually happened
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "If I cannot then I just have to trust that she will take it. There is no proper way to know." (C01, Phase 1, L109)
Reflexivity_note: This is the caregiver's uncertainty, not evidence that the dose was missed.

Definition: A verbal yes may not settle whether dosing occurred.
Subtheme: Handoffs and distance create uncertainty about what actually happened
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "sometimes they say yes I took it but then later I find out they forgot." (C01, Phase 1, L269)
Reflexivity_note: I retained this boundary case but removed the former cross corpus generalization.
Interview_gap: Strongly described in C01 but not systematically probed across households; treat as a boundary case rather than a universal verification failure.

Definition: Shared reminding can fail when all available people are occupied simultaneously.
Subtheme: Routine transitions separate medicines, cues, people, and dose times
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "If one person forgets somebody else usually remembers. But sometimes everyone is busy. That is when the problem happens."
Reflexivity_note: This supports collective lapse, but no household pairing is available.

Definition: Leaving home can separate a person from medicine even when timing is remembered.
Subtheme: Routine transitions separate medicines, cues, people, and dose times
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "There was one time we were going somewhere and later she asked where her medicine was. We had to check the bags."
Reflexivity_note: I kept carrying separate from remembering because they require different designs.

Definition: Travel, guests, and altered meals remove the cues that ordinarily carry dosing.
Subtheme: Routine transitions separate medicines, cues, people, and dose times
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "At home everything is fixed... When you go somewhere the routine changes."
Reflexivity_note: The mechanism is cue displacement, not a global memory deficit.

Definition: Farming, housework, and paid work reorganize attention around tasks rather than dose times.
Subtheme: Routine transitions separate medicines, cues, people, and dose times
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "It gets hardest when I'm super busy with household work—especially in the morning."
Reflexivity_note: Different work settings share temporal instability, not identical burdens.

Definition: Changes in strip appearance, brand, company, or packaging can unsettle recognition built through familiar medicine identity.
Subtheme: Supply and medicine-identity changes create non-reminder failures
Theme: Breakdowns emerge at routine and handoff boundaries, creating uncertainty, burden, and adherence risk
Example_quote: "Medicine packaging can change. Or different company can have different packaging."
Reflexivity_note: Visual cues help only while packaging remains stable.

Definition: A reminder should specify medicine, timing, dose, or relation to food.
Subtheme: Actionable prompts connect reminders to familiar medicine while respecting context
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "It should say which medicine to take and when. [...] Not only saying take medicine." (C01, Phase 1, L209)
Reflexivity_note: Specific content answers the failure of generic alarms, despite elicitation.
Interview_gap: Mostly elicited design expectation; distinguish from actual tool use.

Definition: Pictures and simple time cues connect digital instructions to familiar medicine appearance.
Subtheme: Actionable prompts connect reminders to familiar medicine while respecting context
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "If it shows the medicine picture then they can match it with the medicine they have."
Reflexivity_note: Packaging changes limit this mechanism, so images cannot stand alone.
Interview_gap: Pictures can support matching but packaging changes make image-only identification brittle.

Definition: Technology should complement relational care rather than replace family and community roles.
Subtheme: Delegated setup can support use, but accountable people retain authority
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "It should help the family. Not replace us. It should make checking easier."
Reflexivity_note: This direct account supports relational interdependence, while independent managers bound its reach.
Interview_gap: Supports relational interdependence while independent self-managers bound its reach.

Definition: Trusted kin may enter schedules while older adults retain everyday use.
Subtheme: Delegated setup can support use, but accountable people retain authority
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "I would probably set it up. After that she can just hear it and press one button. I would manage the settings."
Reflexivity_note: Delegation can support participation, but setup authority still needs revocability.
Interview_gap: Settings-control questions were inconsistently asked; retain as formative design evidence, not a prevalence claim.

Definition: Technology may inform or warn but should not recommend medication changes.
Subtheme: Delegated setup can support use, but accountable people retain authority
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "I don't want it to randomly recommend medicines. I want it to show what the doctor prescribed and basic information." (C04, Phase 1, L189)
Reflexivity_note: This boundary is strongly corroborated despite hypothetical prompting.
Interview_gap: Strongly aligned with multiple accounts, but future-system statements are design judgments.

Definition: Trust rises when kin or professionals check system information against the prescription.
Subtheme: Delegated setup can support use, but accountable people retain authority
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "I would check it. I would not just trust it blindly. Maybe compare with the pharmacy or old medicine."
Reflexivity_note: Trust attaches to accountable people rather than the system alone.
Interview_gap: Trust is described through accountable people; this should not be converted into a claim that users distrust automation generally.

Definition: Button phones, shared phones, or limited device ownership can narrow direct interaction and move some digital work to kin.
Subtheme: Device, document, and interaction conditions shape who can participate directly
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "They use button phones... they find smartphone functions harder to use."
Reflexivity_note: This is an infrastructural condition, not an age based incapacity.

Definition: Caregivers should receive meaningful exceptions, not every reminder event.
Subtheme: Escalation should be delayed, selective, visible, and epistemically modest
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "Maybe only if they don't confirm. Otherwise I don't need every reminder. But if they miss then I should know."
Reflexivity_note: A real miss remains technically uncertain without verified sensing or logs.
Interview_gap: Hypothetical preference; a non-confirmation cannot establish a missed dose.

Definition: Older adults should know when family can inspect medication information.
Subtheme: Escalation should be delayed, selective, visible, and epistemically modest
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "I don't think it should secretly check. They should know. It is for helping them." (C01, Phase 1, L325)
Reflexivity_note: Caregiver endorsement cannot substitute for older adult consent.
Interview_gap: Caregiver endorsement does not substitute for older-adult consent; checking visibility was under-probed.

Definition: Families prefer another reminder and time to respond before involving someone else.
Subtheme: Escalation should be delayed, selective, visible, and epistemically modest
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "Maybe after some time one more reminder. If still not taken then maybe it can tell me also." (C01, Phase 1, L221)
Reflexivity_note: The sequence was prompted, so it is an evaluated expectation, not observed practice.

Definition: A generic sound may not identify which medicine or action is due.
Subtheme: Existing aids can create work or signal without completing the handoff
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "It just rings. It does not say what to take." (C04, Phase 1, L93)
Reflexivity_note: The problem is underspecified content, not sound itself.
Interview_gap: Generic-alarm limitation is supported, but reminder designs were often discussed after interviewer prompting.

Definition: Refilling a pillbox created another remembered task and led to abandonment.
Subtheme: Existing aids can create work or signal without completing the handoff
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "We had to put the medicine inside every time and sometimes we forgot to put it there." (C01, Phase 1, L61)
Reflexivity_note: One household cannot support a claim about pillboxes generally.
Interview_gap: Observed in one household; use as a design test for maintenance burden, not a general claim about pillboxes.

Definition: One caregiver reported that alarms and a paper prescription met current needs.
Subtheme: Low-technology practices and refusal remain legitimate baselines
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "The basic phone alarms and keeping the doctor's prescription handy work well for our current needs." (C06, Phase 1, L51)
Reflexivity_note: This countercase prevents a universal technology misfit claim.
Interview_gap: Countercase prevents a deficit narrative; do not frame app adoption as universally necessary.

Definition: Notes, prescriptions, labels, and leaflets can organize complex medication schedules.
Subtheme: Low-technology practices and refusal remain legitimate baselines
Theme: Technology is legitimate when it repairs bounded coordination gaps without displacing situated competence or human authority
Example_quote: "Whenever there's any doubt about timing or doses, I go right back to checking the doctor's paper prescription."
Reflexivity_note: This contradicts the former claim that nothing is written down.
